title: Kenyan Hibiscus Juice
community: Popular along the coast and increasingly nationwide
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Kenyan Hibiscus Juice — dried hibiscus flowers (Rosella) steeped in hot water with ginger and spices, sweetened, and served chilled over ice. The deep crimson colour and tart, cranberry-like flavour make it one of Kenya's most beautiful and refreshing drinks.
longDesc: Hibiscus juice (known as Rosella juice along the Kenyan coast, and as Zobo, Bissap, or Sobolo elsewhere in Africa) is made from the dried calyces of Hibiscus sabdariffa. The dried flowers produce a stunning deep crimson juice with a tart, cranberry-like flavour that is simultaneously refreshing and complex. Along the Kenyan coast, it is particularly beloved, often infused with ginger and cinnamon.
ingredients: 1 cup dried hibiscus flowers (dried rosella calyces)

substitutions.alternative: Hibiscus tea bags — steep 6—8 bags for concentrated colour and flavour

steps: Combine water, hibiscus flowers, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves in a saucepan.
Bring to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer for 10—12 minutes.
Remove from heat. Allow to steep for 10 more minutes.
Strain through a fine mesh strainer, pressing to extract all the juice.
Add sugar while the liquid is still warm. Stir to dissolve.
Add lime juice. Taste and adjust sweetness.
Allow to cool completely then refrigerate until chilled.
Serve over ice with fresh mint.
chefTips: The longer you steep the hibiscus, the more intense the colour and flavour.
Add sugar while warm for easier dissolution.
Ginger and cinnamon are the classic coastal companions — do not skip them.
commonMistakes: Adding sugar to cold liquid — difficult to dissolve.
Over-sweetening — the tart quality is part of the appeal.

faqs.q: Where do I find dried hibiscus flowers?
faqs.a: Available in most Kenyan markets, spice shops, and health food stores. Along the coast they are sold as rosella or uyoga wa maua. In supermarkets, hibiscus tea bags work as a substitute.

cookingScience: Hibiscus calyces contain anthocyanins — the same class of pigments found in blueberries, red cabbage, and purple grapes. These water-soluble pigments produce the brilliant crimson colour and act as potent antioxidants. The tartness comes from hibiscus acid (a form of citric/malic acid blend specific to hibiscus).
sustainabilityTips: Hibiscus plants grow readily in Kenyan gardens.
Spent hibiscus flowers can be composted.
healthBenefits: Exceptionally rich in anthocyanin antioxidants — among the highest of any plant food.
Studies suggest hibiscus tea may help lower blood pressure.
culturalNote: Hibiscus juice has deep roots in Swahili coastal culture and is celebrated across Sub-Saharan Africa under many names. In Kenya, it is particularly associated with coastal refreshment and is increasingly available in Nairobi health stores and restaurants as awareness of its exceptional nutritional profile grows.
